title: Exploring the Wonders of the Pacific Ocean
excerpt: West Coast companies often assume nearshore means early mornings for their engineers. In practice, a Central American team starts its day two hours ahead of San Francisco and still shares six to seven working hours with it.

author.name: Boyo Martínez
author.bio: Boyo leads product and design at NicaSource, where he helps US companies plan, staff and run nearshore engineering teams. He has spent fifteen years shipping digital products with distributed teams across the Americas.

meta.body:
Introduction

West Coast companies often assume nearshore means early mornings for their engineers. In practice, a Central American team starts its day two hours ahead of San Francisco and still shares six to seven working hours with it.

Making Pacific Time Work

Front-load async work

The first two hours of the nearshore day are ideal for focused work: code review, test automation and documentation. When the Pacific team comes online, the queue is already moving.

Late-day pairing

The shared afternoon is perfect for pairing sessions and design reviews. Keep calendars light in the morning and dense in the overlap, and both sides get their best hours.

Rituals That Survive Distance

  • Written stand-ups posted before the overlap begins.
  • A weekly demo where nearshore engineers present their own work.
  • Rotating on-call so incidents are shared, not exported.

We stopped thinking of them as the team in another country and started thinking of them as the team that starts earlier.

Conclusion

Pacific Time clients get the best of both worlds: a head start every morning and a solid block of real-time collaboration every afternoon.
